blocks.content: Practice reading a finished dashboard on Grafana Play. Identify what a dashboard monitors and whether its panels support a clear goal, find a panel's query and data source, interpret its unit, and identify which panels are resource measurements and which are service measurements.

Use the finished dashboards on Grafana Play. The examples include demo data; don't treat their values as operational limits. Inspect settings without saving changes.

Resources:
- [Grafana dashboard best practices](https://grafana.com/docs/grafana/latest/visualizations/dashboards/build-dashboards/best-practices/)
- [Dashboards](https://grafana.com/docs/grafana/latest/visualizations/dashboards/)
- [Panels and visualizations](https://grafana.com/docs/grafana/latest/visualizations/panels-visualizations/)
- [Configure standard options](https://grafana.com/docs/grafana/latest/visualizations/panels-visualizations/configure-standard-options/)
Explore a finished dashboard to work out what it monitors and whether its panels support a clear goal.
Open **Grafana Dashboard** in full-dashboard view.
Read the panel titles and say in one sentence what the dashboard monitors. Then look for the specific information that would help answer that question.
Count the panels whose title alone tells you what they measure. Identify which panels support the dashboard's question and which distract from it, and look for a general-to-specific progression.
You've identified a dashboard goal and assessed its focus and readability. Next, inspect how a panel gets the data that supports that goal.
Explore a panel to find the query inside it, the data source it runs against, and the format its result comes back in.

blocks.title: Find the query and its data source

blocks.content: Open **Base Query (A) - Total CPU Usage** on the **SQL Expressions Showcase** dashboard.
Open the panel menu and select **Edit**. Leave every setting unchanged.
Notice the data source for query **A**. It's a Prometheus data source, so Grafana sends this query to Prometheus.

Read the query: `sum(rate(process_cpu_seconds_total[5m]))`. It selects one metric, `process_cpu_seconds_total`, turns it into a per-second rate, and sums the result across every instance. The data source holds far more data than this. The query reduces it to the one series the panel needs.

Below the query, find the query options and read **Format**. For this panel it's **Time series**, the shape the result comes back in. The visualization decides how that shape is drawn, so the same time series result could feed a graph, a stat, or a gauge.
Return to the panel without saving.
You've found a panel's query, the data source it runs against, and its result format. The query chooses the data. The visualization only presents it.
Explore the Memory gauge to find its unit setting and connect it to the suffix on its value.

blocks.title: Connect the setting to the label

blocks.content: Open the **Memory** gauge and notice the B suffix beside its value.
Open the **Memory** panel menu and select **Edit**. Expand **Standard options** if it's collapsed. Leave the settings unchanged.
Find **Unit** and read its **bytes(IEC)** setting.

The **Memory** panel formats its numeric value as bytes. B means bytes; larger values can use units such as KiB or MiB. Unit formatting changes the display, not the query's data, and doesn't change timestamps into byte values.

Changing bytes to percent wouldn't calculate memory utilization. It would mislabel the existing values. The unit must match what the query measures; a utilization query would need to return a proportion of capacity.
Return to the **Memory** gauge without saving changes.
You've located Unit and distinguished the displayed label from the unchanged data. Match the unit to what the query measures before interpreting a value.
Explore a dashboard and identify which of its panels are USE measurements and which are RED measurements, naming the measurement each one shows.
Open **Sample Website Dashboard** in full-dashboard view.
Find **Memory / CPU** and the **Memory** gauge. These measure a machine's resources, so they belong to the USE method. Both show how much of the resource is in use, which is utilization.

Find **server requests** and **client side full page load**. These measure the service as its users experience it, so they belong to the RED method. Requests over time is the rate. Page load time is the duration.
RED has a third measurement, errors. Look for a panel that counts failing requests. There isn't one, so this dashboard can't tell you whether requests are failing.
The four golden signals name the same three service measurements as RED, as traffic, errors, and latency, and add saturation: how close a resource is to its capacity. No panel here shows that either.

The remaining panels, **logins**, **Google hits**, **Support calls**, and **Sign ups**, are business measurements. Neither method covers them. The methods tell you what a health dashboard needs, not what every dashboard must contain.
You've identified a dashboard's resource and service measurements and spotted what's missing. The question a dashboard answers tells you which method it needs.
